title: SSEBITDA: measuring steady-state profitability of a SaaS company that is spending to grow
summary: Jason Cohen argues EBITDASM (EBITDA plus S&M) is flawed because stopping S&M doesn't freeze revenue and it assumes efficient acquisition. He proposes SSEBITDA = EBITDA + S&M − COC, counting only the S&M needed to replace cancellations. A Profitable Growth Rate falls out of it, letting you justify "spend to grow" precisely.

principles.text: To test whether a growth-spending SaaS is truly profitable, measure profit as if you spent only enough to stay flat.
principles.quote: How profitable would we be, if we were spending only enough to maintain the current state of the company, neither growing nor shrinking?

principles.text: SSEBITDA adds back all S&M but subtracts the Cost of Cancellation, so it works regardless of sales efficiency.
Stopping S&M spend doesn't mean flat revenue; cancellations shrink it, and a shrinking company that looks profitable is dying.
principles.quote: Halting Sales & Marketing does not mean revenue remains flat.

principles.text: Divide SSEBITDA by the cost of a dollar of new revenue to get the growth you can self-fund; faster growth means a known, quantifiable loss.
Don't strip feature-development costs to get a purer steady state; a product that stops evolving isn't steady because the market keeps moving.
principles.quote: A product that never adds a new feature is _not_ in a "steady-state," because the market is changing around it

principles.text: Watch the metric's direction and its component inputs more than its absolute value; the insights and actions come from the inputs.
principles.quote: The overall number is useful as a sort of combined north-star metric, but all the insights and actions come from backing out of the inputs to the number
